properties.name: Historic town centre
properties.description: This is the old market town: a long High Street that forks into West Street and South Street, with Church Street and the lanes around St Martin’s close by. Until the mid-19th century almost everyone in Dorking lived in this tight centre. Many of the buildings are listed, and the streets sit in the Dorking Conservation Area, designated in 1974.
properties.built: The market town grew up from the 12th–13th century along High Street, South Street and West Street. Until the mid-19th century this tight nucleus was almost the whole of Dorking.
properties.style: A mix of historic commercial buildings, many of them listed, with flats and some houses. The streets form the heart of the Dorking Conservation Area (designated 1974).
properties.price_text: Median of 59 standard sales, 2023–2025: £290,000. This figure includes flats as well as houses.
properties.sources: Mole Valley 2010 character appraisal (official areas 6.4, 6.6, 6.7, grouped here); Surrey Extensive Urban Survey: Dorking (2004); Victoria County History, Surrey vol. 3 (1911); Local Plan Appendix 7.
properties.official: 2010 Built-up Areas Character Appraisal sections 6.4, 6.6 and 6.7, grouped for the public map
properties.boundary_note: Approximate. The three official town-centre character areas have been grouped for this public layer. Exact 2010 lines were not available; the polygon follows the historic streets and the conservation area in the centre.
properties.attribution: Contains HM Land Registry data © Crown copyright and database right 2026. This data is licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0.

properties.name: Dene Street
properties.description: Just east of the High Street, Dene Street is treated as its own character area in the council’s 2010 appraisal. It still has listed buildings, and it sits beside the older market streets rather than the later Victorian suburbs further south and east.
properties.built: Part of the historic town immediately east of the centre; the official appraisal treats it as its own character area. A detailed building-period description was not available without the full 2010 text.
properties.style: Historic streets with listed buildings on Dene Street, on the east side of the town centre.
properties.sources: Mole Valley 2010 character appraisal (official area 6.5); National Heritage List entries on Dene Street.
properties.official: 2010 appraisal section 6.5
properties.boundary_note: Approximate, drawn around Dene Street and the immediately adjoining streets named in or next to the official area title.
properties.attribution: Contains HM Land Registry data © Crown copyright and database right 2026. This data is licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0.

properties.name: Rose Hill
properties.description: Rose Hill is Dorking’s first planned housing. From 1831 William Newland laid out 24 plots around a grassy paddock known as The Oval, just behind South Street. The villas, in Italianate and Tudor styles, were finished by 1861, and many are listed. The mock-Tudor arch from South Street is still the way in.
properties.built: Dorking’s first planned housing. William Newland bought the Butter Hill land in 1831 and laid out plots for 24 houses around a central paddock known as The Oval. The estate is described as complete by 1861; villas went up between the late 1830s and 1869.
properties.style: Italianate and Tudor-style villas around the paddock, many of them Grade II listed. A mock-Tudor arch leads in from South Street.
properties.price_text: Too few sales to give a reliable figure.
properties.sources: Allan Brigham, “Rose Hill – adapted from nature…”, Surrey History V(4), 1997; Dorking Local History Group, “Rose Hill and Butter Hill House”; Ettlinger, Jackson and Overell (1991); 2010 appraisal section 6.8.
properties.official: 2010 appraisal section 6.8
properties.boundary_note: Approximate, drawn tightly around Rose Hill, Upper Rose Hill and Butter Hill.
properties.attribution: Contains HM Land Registry data © Crown copyright and database right 2026. This data is licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0.

properties.name: Cotmandene
properties.description: Cotmandene is the old common just south-east of the town centre, famous as a cricket ground. The 2010 appraisal treats the common and the houses around it as their own character area, and the open space itself is strongly protected in the Local Plan.
properties.built: An historic common on the south-east edge of the town centre, long used as a cricket ground. The surrounding housing is part of the official Cotmandene character area; a full period-by-period description of those houses was not available without the 2010 text.
properties.style: Historic open common, with housing around the edges, inside or beside the Dorking Conservation Area.
properties.price_text: Too few sales to give a reliable figure.
properties.sources: 2010 appraisal section 6.9; Victoria County History, Surrey vol. 3 (1911); Dorking Local History Group; Local Plan Policy S4 and Appendix 7.
properties.official: 2010 appraisal section 6.9
properties.boundary_note: Approximate, drawn around the common and the streets that front it. Houses further east are treated as Deepdene unless the official map shows otherwise.
properties.attribution: Contains HM Land Registry data © Crown copyright and database right 2026. This data is licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0.

properties.name: Ansell Road to London Road
properties.description: These streets just north of the High Street were built in the 1890s as smaller terraces and semis. Rothes Road, Ansell Road, Wathen Road, Hart Road and Jubilee Terrace still give the area its late-Victorian, close-knit character.
properties.built: In the 1890s, smaller semi-detached and terraced houses were built north of the High Street for artisans, in Rothes Road, Ansell Road, Wathen Road, Hart Road and Jubilee Terrace.
properties.style: Late-Victorian terraces and modest semi-detached houses, tightly built between the High Street and the railway.
properties.sources: Ettlinger, Jackson and Overell (1991), p. 75; 2010 appraisal section 6.11.
properties.official: 2010 appraisal section 6.11
properties.boundary_note: Approximate, drawn around the named 1890s streets between the High Street and the railway.
properties.attribution: Contains HM Land Registry data © Crown copyright and database right 2026. This data is licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0.

properties.name: Marlborough Hill
properties.description: Marlborough Hill rises just south of the town centre. The council’s 2010 appraisal treats it as its own character area. Marlborough Road and Beresford Road include houses built by the Urban District Council in the 1920s — some of the first municipal housing in the town, after Nower Road in 1920.
properties.built: Marlborough Road and Beresford Road were among the Urban District Council houses built in the 1920s. The official area may also include older or later streets on Marlborough Hill; the full 2010 description was not available.
properties.style: Early-20th-century houses, including 1920s municipal housing on Marlborough and Beresford Roads, on rising ground south of the centre.
properties.sources: Ettlinger, Jackson and Overell (1991), pp. 92–93; 2010 appraisal section 6.10.
properties.official: 2010 appraisal section 6.10
properties.boundary_note: Approximate, drawn around Marlborough Road, Marlborough Hill, Beresford Road and immediately adjoining streets.
properties.attribution: Contains HM Land Registry data © Crown copyright and database right 2026. This data is licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0.

properties.name: Ashcombe Road and the 1930s north
properties.description: North of the railway, the streets around Ashcombe Road were laid out in the 1930s after part of Bradley Farm, on the Denbies estate, was sold. Fairfield Drive belongs to the same period: houses there were built between 1935 and 1939. The official 2010 “Ashcombe Road North” boundary has not been seen, so Fairfield is grouped here as a neighbouring 1930s street, not as a confirmed official line.
properties.built: The sale of part of Bradley Farm, on the Denbies estate, in the 1930s led to building in Ashcombe, Keppel and Calvert Roads. Fairfield Drive is recorded as built between 1935 and 1939.
properties.style: Inter-war suburban houses, including the 1930s streets north of the railway.
properties.sources: Ettlinger, Jackson and Overell (1991), pp. 90–92; Ian Capper, Geograph captions for Fairfield Drive (1935–1939); 2010 appraisal section 7.1.
properties.official: 2010 appraisal section 7.1 (Ashcombe Road North). Fairfield Drive is included here as a 1930s northern street; its official area is not confirmed.
properties.boundary_note: Approximate. Fairfield Drive is included because of its date and position; the official 2010 map may place it in this area or in North Dorking.
properties.attribution: Contains HM Land Registry data © Crown copyright and database right 2026. This data is licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0.

properties.name: North Dorking
properties.description: The 2010 appraisal gives the rest of north Dorking its own character area, separate from the 1930s Ashcombe streets. Much of the land between the High Street and the railway, and the streets north of the stations, was built up from the late 19th century onwards. Fraser Gardens, built in the late 1930s after slum clearance, and named after Sir Malcolm Fraser of Pixham, is in this northern part of town; it is included here pending the official map.
properties.built: The official appraisal separates North Dorking from Ashcombe Road North. A full building-period description was not available without the 2010 text. The streets north of the centre and around the stations filled in mainly from the late 19th and early 20th centuries, after the railway arrived.
properties.style: A mixed northern suburb of late-19th and 20th-century housing, distinct in the official appraisal from the 1930s Ashcombe streets.
properties.price_text: Median of 53 standard sales, 2023–2025: £460,250. This figure includes flats as well as houses.
properties.sources: 2010 appraisal section 7.3; Surrey Extensive Urban Survey: Dorking (2004); Ettlinger, Jackson and Overell (1991), pp. 92–93 (Fraser Gardens; The Times, 19 January 1938).
properties.official: 2010 appraisal section 7.3
properties.boundary_note: Approximate. Used for northern streets not assigned to Ashcombe Road North, Ansell Road to London Road, the station approaches or Pixham. Fraser Gardens is placed here pending the official map.
properties.attribution: Contains HM Land Registry data © Crown copyright and database right 2026. This data is licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0.

properties.name: Pixham
properties.description: Pixham sits on the north-eastern edge of Dorking, official in the 2010 appraisal as its own character area, and with its own conservation-area description along Pixham Lane. Pixham Mill is early 19th century and listed; picturesque cottages, including 17th-century Pixham Mill Cottage, stand nearby. Later streets spread out around it, but Pixham still feels more like a small settlement than a town suburb.
properties.built: A distinct settlement on the north-eastern edge of the town, with 17th-century cottages around Pixham Mill (the mill itself is early 19th century) and later suburban streets.
properties.style: A village-like suburb: historic cottages and the mill along Pixham Lane, with later houses and flats around Leslie Road and Swan Mill Gardens.
properties.price_text: Median of 43 standard sales, 2023–2025: £400,000. This figure includes flats as well as houses.
properties.sources: 2010 appraisal section 7.5; Local Plan Appendix 7, “Pixham Lane, Dorking”; National Heritage List (Pixham Mill, Pixham Mill Cottage).
properties.official: 2010 appraisal section 7.5. Pixham Lane is also described in Local Plan Appendix 7 as a conservation area on the north-eastern edge of Dorking.
properties.boundary_note: The Pixham Lane conservation area uses the official open-data boundary. The wider Pixham residential area around it is approximate.
properties.attribution: Contains HM Land Registry data © Crown copyright and database right 2026. This data is licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0.

properties.name: Hampstead Lane area
properties.description: The Hampstead Lane area, west of the town centre, is its own official character area. Nineteenth-century houses were built along Hampstead Road; later accounts note that many of the poorer houses on Hampstead and Falkland Roads were replaced in the 1960s and 1970s. Falkland Road is shown separately, as in the 2010 appraisal.
properties.built: Nineteenth-century housing along Hampstead Road (and, in the same account, Falkland Road). Many of the poorer-quality 19th-century houses on those roads were replaced in the 1960s and 1970s. Falkland Road is a separate official area, so this description is applied here only to the Hampstead streets.
properties.style: A mix of surviving 19th-century houses and later 20th-century replacements, west of the town centre.
properties.price_text: Too few sales to give a reliable figure.
properties.sources: Ettlinger, Jackson and Overell (1991), p. 75; 2010 appraisal section 8.1.
properties.official: 2010 appraisal section 8.1
properties.boundary_note: Approximate, drawn around Hampstead Road and Hampstead Lane. The official line between this area and the Falkland Road area is not confirmed.
properties.attribution: Contains HM Land Registry data © Crown copyright and database right 2026. This data is licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0.

properties.name: Westcott Road
properties.description: Westcott Road is the western way out of Dorking, treated as its own character area in 2010. The full official description has not been read, so this profile stays cautious. Nower Road, where the Urban District Council built its first houses in 1920, is on this west side of town and is grouped here until the official map is available.
properties.built: The western approach to the town, towards Sondes Place and Westcott. A full period description was not available without the 2010 text. Nower Road, where the Urban District Council built its first houses in 1920, lies on this west side of town and is included here pending the official map.
properties.style: A mixed western approach: larger houses, later infill, and early municipal housing on Nower Road from 1920.
properties.sources: 2010 appraisal section 8.2; Ettlinger, Jackson and Overell (1991), pp. 92–93 (Nower Road, 1920).
properties.official: 2010 appraisal section 8.2
properties.boundary_note: Approximate. Nower Road is included on the west side of town pending the official map.
properties.attribution: Contains HM Land Registry data © Crown copyright and database right 2026. This data is licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0.

properties.name: Deepdene
properties.description: East of the town, the old Deepdene estate was broken up in the 1920s and the land nearest the stations was turned into housing. Deepdene Vale and Deepdene Park date from that inter-war period: large houses in a leafy setting, quite different from the Victorian streets closer to the centre. Punchbowl Lane is included here because it continues that eastward, larger-house character; the official 2010 line may or may not take it in, and the boundary is flagged as approximate.
properties.built: The Deepdene estate was broken up in the 1920s. Land nearest the stations was developed for housing in the 1920s and 1930s, including Deepdene Vale and Deepdene Park, helped by the electrification of the railway.
properties.style: Large 1920s and 1930s houses in a leafy setting east of the town, on former estate land. Some later houses and converted buildings stand along Deepdene Avenue.
properties.sources: Dorking Museum, “The Deepdene” and “Decline of the Deepdene”; Ettlinger, Jackson and Overell (1991), pp. 90–92; Jackson (1988), p. 52; 2010 appraisal section 8.5.
properties.official: 2010 appraisal section 8.5
properties.boundary_note: Approximate. Punchbowl Lane and some Chart Lane addresses are included as neighbouring large-house streets east of Cotmandene; they are not confirmed as inside the official Deepdene area.
properties.attribution: Contains HM Land Registry data © Crown copyright and database right 2026. This data is licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0.

properties.name: Tower Hill
properties.description: Tower Hill, with Arundel and Howard Roads, was laid out between 1850 and 1870 by the National Freehold Land Society — a mid-Victorian planned estate, later than Rose Hill and earlier than the streets around Ridgeway Road.
properties.built: Developed between 1850 and 1870 by the National Freehold Land Society, together with Arundel and Howard Roads.
properties.style: Mid-Victorian houses on a planned freehold-society estate, distinct from the earlier planned villas at Rose Hill and from the later Ridgeway streets.
properties.sources: Ettlinger, Jackson and Overell (1991), p. 75; 2010 appraisal section 9.5.
properties.official: 2010 appraisal section 9.5
properties.boundary_note: Approximate, drawn around Tower Hill, Arundel Road and Howard Road.
properties.attribution: Contains HM Land Registry data © Crown copyright and database right 2026. This data is licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0.

properties.name: St Paul’s Road to Cliftonville
properties.description: South of the centre, St Paul’s Road and Cliftonville belong to the late-Victorian expansion after Holloway Farm was sold in 1870. Cliftonville was named after Joseph Clift, a local chemist. The first houses were up before 1880. The nearby Ridgeway streets are shown separately, as they are in the official appraisal.
properties.built: After Holloway Farm was sold in 1870, houses in Cliftonville (named after its promoter, Joseph Clift, a local chemist) were built around the same time as the first houses in Knoll, Roman and Ridgeway Roads, and before 1880. Ridgeway Road is a separate official area.
properties.style: Late-Victorian suburban houses on the south side of the town.
properties.sources: Ettlinger, Jackson and Overell (1991), p. 75; 2010 appraisal section 9.4.
properties.official: 2010 appraisal section 9.4
properties.boundary_note: Approximate. The official line between this area and the Ridgeway Road area is not confirmed.
properties.attribution: Contains HM Land Registry data © Crown copyright and database right 2026. This data is licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0.

properties.name: Ridgeway Road area
properties.description: On the southern hillside, Knoll, Roman and Ridgeway Roads were started after Holloway Farm was sold in 1870, with the first houses up before 1880. The 2010 appraisal keeps this group separate from Tower Hill and from Cliftonville, and this map follows that split.
properties.built: After Holloway Farm was sold in 1870, the first houses in Knoll, Roman and Ridgeway Roads were built before 1880.
properties.style: Late-Victorian suburban houses on the southern hillside, a little later than the Tower Hill freehold streets.
properties.price_text: Median of 13 standard sales, 2023–2025: £675,000. This figure includes flats as well as houses.
properties.sources: Ettlinger, Jackson and Overell (1991), p. 75; 2010 appraisal section 9.7.
properties.official: 2010 appraisal section 9.7
properties.boundary_note: Approximate, drawn around Ridgeway, Knoll and Roman Roads and immediately adjoining streets.
properties.attribution: Contains HM Land Registry data © Crown copyright and database right 2026. This data is licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0.

properties.name: Falkland Road area
properties.description: The Falkland Road area, officially its own character area, shares a history with nearby Hampstead Road: 19th-century houses, many of which were replaced in the 1960s and 1970s. The two areas are shown separately, as in the 2010 appraisal.
properties.built: Nineteenth-century housing; many of the poorer-quality 19th-century houses on Falkland and Hampstead Roads were replaced in the 1960s and 1970s. Hampstead Road is a separate official area.
properties.style: A mix of surviving 19th-century houses and later 20th-century replacements, on the south-west side of the town.
properties.price_text: Median of 11 standard sales, 2023–2025: £345,000. This figure includes flats as well as houses.
properties.sources: Ettlinger, Jackson and Overell (1991), p. 75; 2010 appraisal section 9.6.
properties.official: 2010 appraisal section 9.6
properties.boundary_note: Approximate. The official line between this area and the Hampstead Lane area is not confirmed.
properties.attribution: Contains HM Land Registry data © Crown copyright and database right 2026. This data is licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0.

properties.name: North Holmwood
properties.description: North Holmwood is part of Dorking in the Local Plan, but it still has the feel of a village. The historic heart is Spook Hill. Later streets include Bentsbrook Road, Holmesdale Road and Inholms Lane, and housing was built on the old brickworks land after it closed in 1983. The council’s 2010 appraisal actually splits this into three character areas — North Holmwood Village, St Johns, and Holmwood Park. Those internal boundaries are not shown here, because the official maps could not be opened; they can be added when the maps are available.
properties.built: The historic village heart is Spook Hill. A parish of Holmwood was created in 1839; North Holmwood’s church of St John dates from the later 19th century (the parish was established in 1875). Later estates include St John’s and housing on the former Dorking Brickworks site, which closed in 1983; the land north of Inholms Lane was then used for residential housing. The 2010 appraisal splits the village into three character areas; those internal lines are not drawn here because the official maps were not available.
properties.style: An older village around Spook Hill, with later 19th- and 20th-century streets and post-1980s housing on the old brickworks land.
properties.sources: 2010 appraisal sections 10.2–10.4; Local Plan settlement hierarchy (Dorking including North Holmwood); Wikipedia/local histories citing the brickworks and Spook Hill, cross-checked with Exploring Surrey’s Past and the Woodland Trust note on the former brickworks.
properties.official: 2010 appraisal sections 10.2–10.4 (North Holmwood Village, St Johns, and Holmwood Park), shown as one public area until official maps are available
properties.boundary_note: Approximate. Combines three official 2010 areas (Village, St Johns, Holmwood Park) pending official maps. Not to be confused with Mid or South Holmwood, or with Beare Green.
properties.attribution: Contains HM Land Registry data © Crown copyright and database right 2026. This data is licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0.

properties.name: Chart Downs
properties.description: Chart Downs, south-east of the town, was built between 1948 and 1952. It is a planned post-war housing area, and the 2010 appraisal treats it as its own character area, separate from neighbouring North Holmwood and from Goodwyns.
properties.built: Built between 1948 and 1952.
properties.style: A planned post-war housing area of mainly houses and maisonettes, south-east of the town.
properties.price_text: Median of 15 standard sales, 2023–2025: £400,000. This figure includes flats as well as houses.
properties.sources: Ettlinger, Jackson and Overell (1991), pp. 92–93; 2010 appraisal section 10.5.
properties.official: 2010 appraisal section 10.5
properties.boundary_note: Approximate, drawn around Chart Downs and the immediately adjoining Chart Gardens streets.
properties.attribution: Contains HM Land Registry data © Crown copyright and database right 2026. This data is licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0.

properties.name: Goodwyns to Rough Rew
properties.description: Goodwyns and Rough Rew, on the southern edge of the town, were built in the late 1950s and 1960s. The first designs were by Clifford Culpin, with later work by William Ryder, including the Wenlock Edge and Linden Lea tower blocks. Linden Lea, at 14 storeys, went up in 1965. The layout and buildings were later praised by Ian Nairn and Nikolaus Pevsner in The Buildings of England.
properties.built: Built in the late 1950s and 1960s by Dorking Urban District Council. Initial designs were by Clifford Culpin; later work was by William Ryder, including the Wenlock Edge and Linden Lea tower blocks. Linden Lea, 14 storeys, was built in 1965.
properties.style: Mid-20th-century housing, with houses and two tower blocks (Wenlock Edge and Linden Lea), on the southern edge of the town.
properties.price_text: Median of 12 standard sales, 2023–2025: £351,500. This figure includes flats as well as houses.
properties.sources: Ettlinger, Jackson and Overell (1991), pp. 92–93; Nairn and Pevsner, The Buildings of England: Surrey (1971), p. 198; 2010 appraisal section 10.6.
properties.official: 2010 appraisal section 10.6
properties.boundary_note: Approximate, drawn around Goodwyns Road, Goodwyns Place, Rough Rew, Linden Lea, Wenlock Edge and immediately adjoining streets.
properties.attribution: Contains HM Land Registry data © Crown copyright and database right 2026. This data is licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0.

properties.name: Westcott historic centre
properties.description: Westcott’s heart is the triangular village green, with shops and community buildings clustered around it. Much of this centre is a conservation area. The village expanded at the end of the 19th century, so parts have a strong Victorian character, alongside earlier cottages in Westcott Street and a few larger early-19th-century houses on the Guildford Road.
properties.built: A village with medieval origins and a tight historic centre around a triangular green. A considerable expansion at the end of the 19th century gives parts of the centre a strong Victorian character. Earlier vernacular buildings include The Barracks, a 17th-century building, and 17th- and 18th-century cottages in Westcott Street. There are also early-19th-century houses in larger gardens on the Guildford Road.
properties.style: A tight-knit historic and Victorian village core around the green, with a mix of cottages, later Victorian houses and a few larger early-19th-century houses.
properties.sources: Westcott Neighbourhood Development Plan (2017); Local Plan Appendix 7, Westcott Conservation Area; 2013 Larger Rural Villages Character Appraisal (existence of official internal areas; maps not read).
properties.official: Westcott Conservation Area (Local Plan Appendix 7) used as a stand-in for the historic/Victorian core. The 2013 Larger Rural Villages Character Appraisal splits Westcott into character areas; those official sub-area names and maps were not available.
properties.boundary_note: official conservation-area boundary
properties.attribution: Contains HM Land Registry data © Crown copyright and database right 2026. This data is licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0.

properties.name: Westcott later streets
properties.description: Away from the green, Westcott has a different, later character. From the 1960s the village added streets such as Pointers Hill, Dairy Close, Rokefield (a former nursing home), The Pound and St John’s Court, with more recent houses at Pipp Brook Place and Meadow Close. The Neighbourhood Plan also describes compact development around St John’s Road and Ashley Road, to the north-east.
properties.built: From the 1960s onwards Westcott gained a series of housing developments, including Pointers Hill, Dairy Close (a mixed-affordability development), Rokefield (a former nursing home), The Pound, St John’s Court, and smaller 21st-century schemes such as Pipp Brook Place and Meadow Close. The north-east of the village, around St John’s Road and Ashley Road, is described as relatively compact.
properties.style: Later 20th- and early 21st-century housing estates and cul-de-sacs, distinct from the historic and Victorian centre.
properties.sources: Westcott Neighbourhood Development Plan (2017), sections 3.1, 5.4.4 and sustainability appendix.
properties.official: Standing in for later 20th-century parts of Westcott described in the Neighbourhood Plan, pending the 2013 official character-area map.
properties.boundary_note: Approximate. Covers later Westcott streets outside the conservation area and outside Milton Street, pending the official 2013 character-area map.
properties.attribution: Contains HM Land Registry data © Crown copyright and database right 2026. This data is licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0.

properties.name: Milton Street
properties.description: Milton Street is a small historic group of its own, east of Westcott, with a separate conservation area. It is part of Westcott parish, but it is not just another street in the village — the Neighbourhood Plan treats it as an outlying place, and this map does the same.
properties.built: A separate historic group to the east of Westcott village, with its own conservation area. The Neighbourhood Plan treats it as outlying from the village core.
properties.style: A small historic hamlet of traditional buildings, separate from Westcott’s later streets.
properties.price_text: Too few sales to give a reliable figure.
properties.sources: Local Plan Appendix 7, Milton Street Conservation Area; Westcott Neighbourhood Development Plan (2017).
properties.official: Milton Street Conservation Area (Local Plan Appendix 7), in Westcott parish, east of the village.
properties.boundary_note: official conservation-area boundary
properties.attribution: Contains HM Land Registry data © Crown copyright and database right 2026. This data is licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0.

properties.name: Brockham village green
properties.description: Brockham is organised around its large village green, which still sets the character of the historic centre. The conservation area description notes that 20th-century housing to the north and south left this core little changed: cottages on the north side of the green, a Victorian vicarage and school, and 19th-century semis on the edge, with Box Hill as the backdrop.
properties.built: The historic village is gathered around a large green. Appendix 7 notes that 20th-century housing to the north and south of the green left the core little changed. Buildings include tight cottages on the north side of the green, a Victorian vicarage and school, and 19th-century semi-detached cottages on the edge.
properties.style: A picturesque village-green setting, with cottages, later modest houses, and a largely unchanged historic core.
properties.sources: Local Plan Appendix 7, Brockham Conservation Area; 2013 Larger Rural Villages Character Appraisal (official internal areas exist; maps not read).
properties.official: Brockham Conservation Area (Local Plan Appendix 7), used as a stand-in for the historic core pending the 2013 character-area map.
properties.boundary_note: official conservation-area boundary
properties.attribution: Contains HM Land Registry data © Crown copyright and database right 2026. This data is licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0.

properties.name: Brockham later streets
properties.description: Around the old green, Brockham has later 20th-century streets — the conservation-area description already notes housing to the north and south of the green. Those later streets are shown separately here, pending the official 2013 character-area map.
properties.built: Twentieth-century housing to the north and south of the village green, noted in the conservation-area description as leaving the historic core little changed.
properties.style: Later suburban streets and estates around the historic village, including roads such as Tanners Meadow and Oakdene Road.
properties.sources: Local Plan Appendix 7, Brockham Conservation Area (notes 20th-century housing north and south of the green).
properties.official: Standing in for later 20th-century parts of Brockham outside the conservation area, pending the 2013 official character-area map.
properties.boundary_note: Approximate. Covers Brockham addresses outside the conservation area and outside Strood Green, pending the 2013 map.
properties.attribution: Contains HM Land Registry data © Crown copyright and database right 2026. This data is licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0.

properties.name: Strood Green
properties.description: Strood Green is included with Brockham as a large village in the Local Plan, but it is a place of its own, with its own recreation ground. It is shown separately here, rather than as part of the village green.
properties.built: A separate built-up area from historic Brockham. A full period description was not found in the sources read for this note.
properties.style: A small residential area adjoining Brockham, treated separately because official policy already names it in its own right.
properties.sources: Mole Valley Local Plan settlement hierarchy and Policy EN3; Local Plan local green space list (Strood Green Recreation Ground).
properties.official: Named in the Local Plan as part of the large village “Brockham (including Strood Green)”, but a distinct built area with its own recreation ground.
properties.boundary_note: Approximate, drawn around the Strood Green residential streets. No official character-area map was available.
properties.attribution: Contains HM Land Registry data © Crown copyright and database right 2026. This data is licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0.

properties.name: Capel
properties.description: Capel is a long, slightly winding village along The Street, with a spur down Vicarage Lane. In the conservation area, 17th-century Wealden cottages, Victorian cottages and later houses stand close together, among shops, community buildings and the pubs — the mix typical of a working Surrey village. The 2013 official appraisal does split Capel into character areas; those internal lines are not drawn here because the maps could not be opened.
properties.built: A linear village along The Street, with a spur along Vicarage Lane. The conservation area mixes 17th-century Wealden cottages, Victorian cottages and later housing “cheek-by-jowl”, with larger historic buildings such as Churchgardens Farmhouse and The Red House.
properties.style: A long village street of mixed periods, from Wealden cottages to later 20th-century houses, rather than a single planned estate.
properties.sources: Local Plan Appendix 7, Capel Conservation Area; 2013 Larger Rural Villages Character Appraisal (internal areas exist; maps not read); Local Plan Policy EN3 (Tier 3 inset village).
properties.official: Capel Conservation Area plus the wider inset village. The 2013 appraisal has official internal character areas; those names and maps were not available, so the village is shown as one area.
properties.boundary_note: The conservation area uses the official boundary. The rest of the village is an approximate envelope of Capel addresses. Official 2013 internal splits are not shown.

properties.name: Beare Green
properties.description: Beare Green is one of the district’s large villages, inset from the Green Belt, and it has its own station (Holmwood). It is not a conservation area, and it should not be confused with North, Mid or South Holmwood. The 2013 official appraisal splits it into character areas; those internal lines are not shown here because the maps could not be opened.
properties.built: A larger village near Holmwood Station, not a conservation area. A detailed period-by-period description was not available without the 2013 appraisal text.
properties.style: A 20th-century village of mixed housing, distinct from Mid and South Holmwood and from North Holmwood.
properties.sources: Mole Valley Local Plan settlement hierarchy and Policy EN3; 2013 Larger Rural Villages Character Appraisal, section 4.3 (internal areas exist; maps not read).
properties.official: Tier 3 large inset village, with official 2013 character areas (section 4.3 of the Larger Rural Villages appraisal). Those sub-area names and maps were not available, so the village is shown as one area.
properties.boundary_note: Approximate envelope of Beare Green addresses. Official 2013 internal splits are not shown.
properties.attribution: Contains HM Land Registry data © Crown copyright and database right 2026. This data is licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0.

properties.name: Betchworth
properties.description: Betchworth is a small village strung along The Street, with a conservation area at its heart. The official description is of an irregular scatter of houses, mostly of 17th- and 18th-century character, with later buildings discreetly placed, and strong brick walls around Betchworth House and the churchyard.
properties.built: An irregular scatter of mainly domestic buildings along The Street. The conservation-area description says modern developments have been discreetly sited, and that the traditional architectural character of the 17th and 18th centuries predominates.
properties.style: A small historic village along The Street, with brick walls a strong feature, especially around Betchworth House and the churchyard.
properties.sources: Local Plan Appendix 7, Betchworth Conservation Area; Local Plan Policy EN3 (Tier 4).
properties.official: Tier 4 small village; Betchworth Conservation Area, Local Plan Appendix 7.
properties.boundary_note: The conservation area uses the official boundary. The rest of the village is an approximate envelope of Betchworth addresses.
properties.attribution: Contains HM Land Registry data © Crown copyright and database right 2026. This data is licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0.

properties.name: Newdigate
properties.description: Newdigate is a small Green Belt village with a conservation area at its core. It is shown as one place here. The 2013 larger-village appraisal does not cover it; a finer split can be added if the Landscape SPD or a later study clearly supports one.
properties.built: A small rural village with a historic core in the conservation area. A full period-by-period description of later streets was not read in this research.
properties.style: A small Wealden village with a historic centre and later houses around it.
properties.sources: Local Plan Appendix 7, Newdigate Conservation Area; Local Plan Policy EN3 (Tier 4).
properties.official: Tier 4 small village with a conservation area (Local Plan Appendix 7). Not in the 2013 larger-villages appraisal. Shown as one area.
properties.boundary_note: The conservation area uses the official boundary. The rest of the village is an approximate envelope of Newdigate addresses.
properties.attribution: Contains HM Land Registry data © Crown copyright and database right 2026. This data is licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0.

properties.name: Ockley
properties.description: Ockley is a linear village along the A29, looking towards the wooded slopes of Leith Hill, with a green edged by horse chestnuts. The conservation area covers this historic roadside collection of buildings. It is shown as one place, pending any later official split.
properties.built: A linear village along the A29 (Stane Street), in a strong landscape setting under Leith Hill, with a village green.
properties.style: A linear village of traditional buildings along the main road, with a green (horse chestnuts on the east side) and a broad countryside setting.
properties.sources: Local Plan Appendix 7, Ockley Conservation Area; Local Plan Policy EN3 (Tier 4).
properties.official: Tier 4 small village; Ockley Conservation Area, Local Plan Appendix 7.
properties.boundary_note: The conservation area uses the official boundary. The rest of the village is an approximate envelope of Ockley addresses.
properties.attribution: Contains HM Land Registry data © Crown copyright and database right 2026. This data is licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0.

properties.name: Mickleham
properties.description: Mickleham is a small village in the Mole Gap, with its own conservation area. It sits close to Westhumble, but the Local Plan lists the two as separate villages, and this map does the same.
properties.built: A small village in the Mole Gap, with a conservation area. Shown separately from neighbouring Westhumble, as in the Local Plan.
properties.style: A small historic Downs-edge village, not merged with Westhumble.
properties.sources: Local Plan Appendix 7 (Mickleham Conservation Area); Local Plan Policy EN3 (Tier 4).
properties.official: Tier 4 small village; Mickleham Conservation Area.
properties.boundary_note: The conservation area uses the official boundary. The rest of the village is an approximate envelope of Mickleham addresses.
properties.attribution: Contains HM Land Registry data © Crown copyright and database right 2026. This data is licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0.

properties.name: Westhumble
properties.description: Westhumble is a small village just north of Dorking, in the Mole Gap. It has no conservation area in the Local Plan list, and it is not the same place as Mickleham, even though the two sit close together. Both are shown in their own right.
properties.built: A small village in the Mole Gap, listed separately from Mickleham in the Local Plan. A full period-by-period character appraisal was not read (the 2013 Landscape SPD, which covers smaller settlements, was not available).
properties.style: A small residential village in the Mole Gap, without a designated conservation area.
properties.sources: Mole Valley Local Plan settlement hierarchy and Policy EN3 (Tier 4). Appendix 7 has no Westhumble conservation area.
properties.official: Tier 4 small village. No conservation area is listed for Westhumble in Local Plan Appendix 7.
properties.boundary_note: Approximate envelope of Westhumble addresses. No official character-area or conservation-area boundary was available.
properties.attribution: Contains HM Land Registry data © Crown copyright and database right 2026. This data is licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0.

properties.name: Holmbury St Mary
properties.description: Holmbury St Mary is a hill village with its own conservation area. It is not named in the Local Plan’s village hierarchy, but it is clearly a place in its own right, and it is not shown here as part of Abinger Hammer or Abinger Common.
properties.built: A distinct hill village with its own conservation area, separate from Abinger Hammer and Abinger Common.
properties.style: A small historic village in the Surrey Hills, with its own conservation area.
properties.sources: Local Plan Appendix 7, Holmbury St Mary Conservation Area.
properties.official: Holmbury St Mary Conservation Area (Local Plan Appendix 7). Not named in the Local Plan settlement hierarchy; treated here as its own small village, not as part of Abinger.
properties.boundary_note: The conservation area uses the official boundary. The rest of the village is an approximate envelope of Holmbury St Mary addresses.
properties.attribution: Contains HM Land Registry data © Crown copyright and database right 2026. This data is licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0.

properties.name: Abinger Hammer
properties.description: Abinger Hammer is a small valley village of mainly 19th-century buildings along the A25. The green and cricket ground sit on the south side of the road, and a tight cluster of buildings gathers at the junction with Hackhurst Lane. It is not the same place as Abinger Common or Holmbury St Mary.
properties.built: A small village of mainly 19th-century buildings along the A25, contained in a valley, with the village green and cricket ground on the south side of the road.
properties.style: A linear 19th-century village in a valley, with a green and cricket ground, and a tight cluster of buildings at the Hackhurst Lane junction.
properties.price_text: Too few sales to give a reliable figure.
properties.sources: Local Plan Appendix 7, Abinger Hammer Conservation Area; Local Plan settlement hierarchy (Tier 4).
properties.official: Tier 4 small village; Abinger Hammer Conservation Area, Local Plan Appendix 7.
properties.boundary_note: The conservation area uses the official boundary. The rest of the village is an approximate envelope of Abinger Hammer addresses.
properties.attribution: Contains HM Land Registry data © Crown copyright and database right 2026. This data is licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0.

properties.name: Abinger Common
properties.description: Abinger Common is a small rural community, listed separately from Abinger Hammer in the Local Plan. It is shown on its own, rather than as part of a single “Abinger” area.
properties.built: A small rural community, officially distinct from Abinger Hammer. A full conservation-area or character-appraisal description of the whole settlement was not used here (Friday Street and Broadmoor nearby have their own conservation areas as hamlets).
properties.style: A small, loose-knit rural community in the Surrey Hills.
properties.price_text: Too few sales to give a reliable figure.
properties.sources: Mole Valley Local Plan settlement hierarchy (Tier 5, other rural communities).
properties.official: Tier 5 “other rural community” in the Local Plan, separate from Abinger Hammer.
properties.boundary_note: Approximate envelope of Abinger Common addresses. Nearby Friday Street and Broadmoor conservation areas are not absorbed into this polygon.
properties.attribution: Contains HM Land Registry data © Crown copyright and database right 2026. This data is licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0.

properties.name: Mid Holmwood
properties.description: Mid Holmwood is a small community along the Horsham Road, officially an “other rural community” in the Local Plan. It is not part of Dorking, and it is not the same place as North Holmwood, South Holmwood or Beare Green.
properties.built: A small roadside community on the A24 / Horsham Road, historically distinct from North and South Holmwood. A full character appraisal was not read.
properties.style: A small linear settlement along the Horsham Road.
properties.price_text: Too few sales to give a reliable figure.
properties.sources: Mole Valley Local Plan settlement hierarchy (Tier 5).
properties.official: Tier 5 “other rural community”. Not part of Dorking, and not the same place as North or South Holmwood or Beare Green.
properties.boundary_note: Approximate envelope of Mid Holmwood addresses.
properties.attribution: Contains HM Land Registry data © Crown copyright and database right 2026. This data is licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0.

properties.name: South Holmwood
properties.description: South Holmwood is a small village of its own, officially a Tier 4 village in the Local Plan, south of Holmwood Common. A church was built here in 1838. It is not part of Dorking, and it is not the same place as Mid Holmwood, North Holmwood or Beare Green.
properties.built: A small village south of Holmwood Common. St Mary Magdalene church was built in 1838, with a school following in 1844. Later roadside housing includes streets such as Warwick Road and Warwick Close (from recent sales data; those street names are used only to help place the area, not as a complete historic account).
properties.style: A small village and roadside settlement, separate from Beare Green and from North Holmwood.
properties.sources: Mole Valley Local Plan Policy EN3 (Tier 4); Exploring Surrey’s Past, Holmwood (church 1838, school 1844).
properties.official: Tier 4 small village. Not part of Dorking, and not the same place as North or Mid Holmwood or Beare Green.
properties.boundary_note: Approximate envelope of South Holmwood / Holmwood-locality addresses that are not in Mid Holmwood, North Holmwood or Beare Green.
